vjimc-2012-cat1-01.title: Intermediate value theorem and mean value theorem
vjimc-2012-cat1-01.body:
**Existence.** $f$ is differentiable, hence continuous. Let $g(x)=f(x)-x$ and $h(x)=f(x)-(1-x)$, both continuous on $[0,1]$. Since $0\le f\le1$:
$$g(0)=f(0)\ge0,\quad g(1)=f(1)-1\le0,\qquad h(0)=f(0)-1\le0,\quad h(1)=f(1)\ge0 .$$
By the intermediate value theorem there are $\alpha,\beta\in[0,1]$ with $g(\alpha)=0$ and $h(\beta)=0$, i.e. $f(\alpha)=\alpha$, $f(\beta)=1-\beta$.

**Uniqueness of $\alpha$.** Suppose $f(\alpha)=\alpha$ and $f(\alpha')=\alpha'$ with $\alpha<\alpha'$. By the mean value theorem there is $\theta\in(\alpha,\alpha')$ with
$$f'(\theta)=\frac{f(\alpha')-f(\alpha)}{\alpha'-\alpha}=\frac{\alpha'-\alpha}{\alpha'-\alpha}=1,$$
contradicting $|f'(\theta)|\ne1$.

**Uniqueness of $\beta$.** If $f(\beta)=1-\beta$ and $f(\beta')=1-\beta'$ with $\beta<\beta'$, the mean value theorem gives $\theta'$ with
$$f'(\theta')=\frac{(1-\beta')-(1-\beta)}{\beta'-\beta}=-1,$$
again a contradiction. ∎

vjimc-2012-cat1-01.title: Darboux's theorem: $g$ and $h$ are strictly monotone
vjimc-2012-cat1-01.body:
Existence is as in the first solution. For uniqueness we show that $g(x)=f(x)-x$ and $h(x)=f(x)+x-1$ are strictly monotone.

By Darboux's theorem, a derivative has the intermediate value property. Since $g'=f'-1$ never vanishes on $[0,1]$, it cannot take both signs (otherwise it would take the value $0$ in between). So $g'>0$ everywhere or $g'<0$ everywhere, and $g$ is strictly monotone; it has at most one zero. Similarly $h'=f'+1\ne0$ has constant sign, so $h$ is strictly monotone and has at most one zero. Hence $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are unique. ∎

vjimc-2012-cat1-02.title: Cayley–Hamilton
vjimc-2012-cat1-02.body:
**Answer:** $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&11\\11&101\end{pmatrix}$ or $A=\begin{pmatrix}101&11\\11&2\end{pmatrix}$.

Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}p_1&p_2\\p_3&p_4\end{pmatrix}=B^2$ with all $p_i$ prime and $d=\det B=q^2$, $q$ prime. Let $t=\operatorname{tr}B$. By Cayley–Hamilton, $B^2=tB-dI$, so
$$tB=A+dI=\begin{pmatrix}p_1+d&p_2\\p_3&p_4+d\end{pmatrix}. \tag{1}$$
If $t=0$ then $A=-dI$, whose entries are not primes. Replacing $B$ by $-B$ if needed, assume $t>0$.

**The trace.** Taking traces in (1): $t^2=p_1+p_4+2d\ge2+2+2\cdot4=12$, so $t\ge4$. By (1), $t$ divides the off-diagonal entries $p_2$ and $p_3$ (as $B$ is an integer matrix); since they are primes and $t>1$, $t=p_2=p_3$. Hence
$$B=\begin{pmatrix}a&1\\1&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad a=\frac{p_1+d}{t},\ b=\frac{p_4+d}{t}\in\mathbb Z_{>0},$$
and
$$A=B^2=\begin{pmatrix}a^2+1&a+b\\a+b&b^2+1\end{pmatrix},\qquad d=ab-1 .$$

**Parity.** If $a^2+1$ and $b^2+1$ were both odd, $a$ and $b$ would be even and $a+b$ even. So one of the three primes $a^2+1$, $b^2+1$, $a+b$ is even, i.e. equals $2$. Since $ab=d+1=q^2+1\ge5$, $\max(a,b)\ge3$ and $a+b\ge4$. So $a^2+1=2$ or $b^2+1=2$, i.e. $a=1$ or $b=1$.

**Case $a=1$.** Then $d=b-1=q^2$ and $p_2=a+b=q^2+2$. If $q\ne3$, then $q^2\equiv1\pmod3$, so $3\mid q^2+2$, forcing $q^2+2=3$, $q=1$ — not prime. Hence $q=3$, $b=10$, and
$$B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&10\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=B^2=\begin{pmatrix}2&11\\11&101\end{pmatrix},$$
where indeed $2,11,101$ are prime and $\det B=9=3^2$.

**Case $b=1$** is symmetric and gives $A=\begin{pmatrix}101&11\\11&2\end{pmatrix}$.

Both matrices satisfy the conditions, so these are all. ∎

vjimc-2012-cat1-03.title: Substitution and Cauchy–Schwarz
vjimc-2012-cat1-03.body:
**Answer: $C=\sqrt2$** (the left side is always $<\sqrt2$ and gets arbitrarily close to it).

**Substitution.** Put $a=\frac1{x+1}$, $b=\frac1{y+1}$, $c=\frac1{z+1}$. Then $a,b,c\in(0,1)$, $a+b+c=1$, and $x=\frac{1-a}{a}=\frac{b+c}{a}$, $y=\frac{c+a}{b}$, $z=\frac{a+b}{c}$. The first term becomes
$$\frac{x}{\sqrt{yz}}\cdot\frac1{x+1}=\frac{b+c}{a}\sqrt{\frac{bc}{(c+a)(a+b)}}\cdot a=\frac{(b+c)\sqrt{bc}}{\sqrt{(c+a)(a+b)}},$$
and similarly for the others. Multiplying by $\sqrt{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}$, the claim "$\text{LHS}<\sqrt2$" is equivalent to
$$\sum_{\text{cyc}}(b+c)\sqrt{bc(b+c)}<\sqrt2\,(a+b+c)\sqrt{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}, \tag{1}$$
where we inserted the factor $a+b+c=1$.

**Proof of (1).** By Cauchy–Schwarz,
$$\sum_{\text{cyc}}(b+c)\sqrt{bc(b+c)}\le\sqrt{\sum_{\text{cyc}}(b+c)^2}\cdot\sqrt{\sum_{\text{cyc}}bc(b+c)} .$$
Now
$$\sum_{\text{cyc}}(b+c)^2<\sum_{\text{cyc}}(b+c)^2+2(ab+bc+ca)=2(a+b+c)^2,$$
$$\sum_{\text{cyc}}bc(b+c)<\sum_{\text{cyc}}bc(b+c)+2abc=(a+b)(b+c)(c+a).$$
Multiplying the square roots gives (1). So the left side of the original inequality is always $<\sqrt2$, and $C=\sqrt2$ works.

**Sharpness.** Take $x=y=t>1$; the constraint gives $\frac{1}{z+1}=1-\frac2{t+1}=\frac{t-1}{t+1}$, i.e. $z=\frac{2}{t-1}$. The expression equals
$$\frac{2}{t+1}\sqrt{\frac tz}+\frac{z}{t}\cdot\frac{1}{z+1}=\sqrt2\,\frac{\sqrt{t(t-1)}}{t+1}+\frac{2}{t(t+1)}\xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{}\sqrt2 .$$
So no $C<\sqrt2$ works, and the smallest constant is $C=\sqrt2$. ∎

vjimc-2012-cat1-04.title: Last digits repeat with period 4; leading digits via logarithms
vjimc-2012-cat1-04.body:
**Answer: all positive integers not divisible by $10$.**

**Multiples of 10 fail.** If $10\mid n$, every $n^k$ ends in $0$ but starts with a nonzero digit.

**Last digit.** $n^5-n=(n-1)n(n+1)(n^2+1)$ is even, and divisible by $5$ (if $n\equiv0,\pm1\pmod5$ one of the first three factors is, and if $n\equiv\pm2$ then $n^2+1\equiv0$). So $10\mid n^5-n$, and then $10\mid n^{4m}(n^5-n)=n^{4(m+1)+1}-n^{4m+1}$. Hence every $n^{4m+1}$ ($m\ge0$) has the same last digit $c$ as $n$; if $10\nmid n$ then $c\in\{1,\dots,9\}$.

**Leading digit.** A positive integer $N$ starts with digit $c$ iff $c\cdot10^j\le N<(c+1)10^j$ for some $j$, i.e. iff the fractional part $\{\log_{10}N\}$ lies in $I_c=[\log_{10}c,\log_{10}(c+1))$, an interval of length $\ell=\log_{10}(1+1/c)>0$.

If $n=1$, then $n^1=1$ works. Let $n\ge2$, $10\nmid n$. Then $\theta=4\log_{10}n$ is irrational: if $n^{4b}=10^{a}$ with positive integers $a,b$, unique factorisation forces $n=2^i5^j$ with $4bi=a=4bj$, so $i=j\ge1$ and $10\mid n$. We need $m\ge0$ with
$$\{\log_{10}n+m\theta\}\in I_c .$$

**Density lemma.** *If $\theta$ is irrational, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every interval $J\subset[0,1)$ of length $\varepsilon$ and every real $\gamma$, some $m\ge0$ has $\{\gamma+m\theta\}\in J$.* Proof: choose an integer $K>1/\varepsilon$. Among the $K+1$ numbers $\{i\theta\}$, $0\le i\le K$, which are distinct (by irrationality), two lie in the same of the $K$ intervals $[\frac{r}{K},\frac{r+1}{K})$; so there is $1\le q\le K$ with $\{q\theta\}=\delta$ or $1-\delta$ where $0<\delta<\frac1K<\varepsilon$. Then the points $\{\gamma+jq\theta\}$, $j=0,1,2,\dots$, move around the circle $[0,1)$ in steps of exactly $\delta$ (all in the same direction), so they cannot jump over an interval of length $\varepsilon>\delta$; hence one of them lies in $J$. $\square$

Applying the lemma with $\gamma=\log_{10}n$, $J=I_c$, we obtain $m$ such that $n^{4m+1}$ starts with $c$ and ends with $c$. So $k=4m+1$ works.

(Example: $n=19$: $19^4=130321$ already starts and ends with $1$; for $n=2$, $k=1$ works trivially.) ∎
